chapter_title: Introduction to Red Hat OpenStack Platform Architecture
chapter_summary:
Welcome to the Red Hat OpenStack Platform, a robust and scalable open-source cloud operating system that controls large pools of compute, storage, and networking resources throughout a datacenter, managing them through a unified dashboard or API. As a Red Hat Certified Architect, understanding OpenStack's intricate architecture is paramount for designing resilient and efficient private cloud solutions. At its core, OpenStack is a collection of interoperating services, each responsible for a specific domain. These services communicate primarily through a message queue (RabbitMQ is commonly used) and store their state in a database (MariaDB or PostgreSQL).

Let's begin by exploring the foundational components. **Keystone** is the Identity service, providing authentication and authorization for all OpenStack services. Without Keystone, no other service can function, as it acts as the central directory for users, projects (tenants), and roles. **Nova** is the Compute service, the heart of any cloud, responsible for managing the lifecycle of virtual machine instances. It orchestrates the scheduling and provisioning of VMs onto hypervisors, handling everything from boot-up to termination. **Glance** is the Image service, acting as a repository for virtual disk images. These images are templates used to create new virtual machines, and Glance ensures their availability and integrity across the cloud. **Neutron** is the Networking service, providing network connectivity as a service. It enables users to create and manage virtual networks, subnets, routers, floating IPs, and security groups, effectively isolating and connecting tenant workloads.

Moving to storage, **Cinder** is the Block Storage service, offering persistent block storage volumes to virtual machines. These volumes can be attached, detached, and snapshot, providing durable storage independent of the VM's lifecycle. For object storage, OpenStack provides **Swift**, which is a highly available, distributed, eventually consistent object storage system, ideal for unstructured data like backups, archives, and media files. While Swift is a core OpenStack component, Red Hat often integrates **Ceph Storage** as a unified storage solution for block (Cinder), object (Swift API), and file storage (Manila). Ceph offers superior performance, scalability, and data protection through replication and erasure coding, making it a preferred choice for enterprise OpenStack deployments. Finally, **Horizon** is the Dashboard service, a web-based graphical user interface that allows administrators and users to interact with OpenStack services, managing instances, networks, volumes, and more through an intuitive interface.

Red Hat's specific implementation, Red Hat OpenStack Platform (RHOSP), brings enterprise-grade stability, support, and additional tooling to the upstream OpenStack project. A key differentiator is the use of **TripleO (OpenStack on OpenStack)** for deployment and management. TripleO leverages OpenStack components (like Nova, Neutron, Glance, Keystone) to deploy and manage the OpenStack control plane itself. This "undercloud" deploys and manages the "overcloud," which is the actual production OpenStack environment. This approach ensures consistency, automation, and simplifies complex deployments, upgrades, and scaling operations. Furthermore, RHOSP emphasizes integration with other Red Hat technologies like Red Hat Ceph Storage, Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform for day-2 operations, and Red Hat Satellite for lifecycle management, creating a comprehensive and robust private cloud ecosystem. Understanding how these components fit together and their interdependencies is crucial for designing a highly available and scalable OpenStack environment, where services are distributed across multiple nodes, often in an active-active configuration, to eliminate single points of failure and ensure continuous operation.

screens.title: Introduction to Red Hat OpenStack Platform Architecture
screens.subtitle: Core services, interactions, and Red Hat's enterprise deployment approach

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will build a clear mental model of Red Hat OpenStack Platform, why it exists, and the pieces you must manage as an architect. OpenStack is a set of interoperating services that together control compute, storage, and networking resources across a datacenter. Each service has a focused responsibility: identity, compute lifecycle, images, networking, block and object storage, and the dashboard. Behind the scenes they coordinate through a message queue and a central state database. Red Hat's distribution adds production tools and a deployment model called TripleO, where an "undercloud" OpenStack deploys and manages the production "overcloud." That approach gives you consistent, automatable deployments, and integrates with Ceph for unified storage and Ansible for day-two operations. As you work through the lesson, notice how service roles limit failure domains and how integrating Ceph changes storage trade-offs. By the end you should be able to name the core services, explain their interactions, and describe why TripleO and Red Hat integrations matter in enterprise clouds. Consider how these design choices reduce manual steps and raise predictability in large deployments.

keyIdea.title: Why architecture matters
keyIdea.text: OpenStack is modular: each service handles a single domain and communicates via messaging and a shared database. Red Hat packages and automates these pieces for reliable, scalable private clouds.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These four objectives orient your learning so you can act as an architect for Red Hat OpenStack Platform. First, you will identify the core services and name their functions. This factual recall matters because correct service identification prevents misconfigured roles and misplaced troubleshooting. For example, knowing Nova is responsible for instance lifecycle prevents you from trying to change compute behavior via the image service. Second, you will explain how services interact and depend on each other through a message queue and a shared database. That understanding helps you reason about failure modes and order of operations during upgrades. Third, you will describe a high-level architecture for a highly available and scalable deployment—this includes control plane distribution, storage backends like Ceph, and active-active patterns. Finally, you will understand Red Hat’s value-add: TripleO deployment automation, certified storage integration, and tools for day-two operations. Each objective includes a small competency milestone so you can verify your understanding by mapping services to scenarios. Keep these outcomes in mind as you move through the lesson content and hands-on activity.

keyIdea.text: Identify services, explain interactions, design HA overclouds, and describe Red Hat's enterprise tooling and integrations.

narration.text: This second objectives slide elaborates how you will apply knowledge. You will practice inspecting service endpoints and interpreting the results to verify deployment health. That practical skill matters because service endpoints are the first place to look when an A P I fails or when a role is misrouted. For instance, listing endpoints with the OpenStack client reveals public, internal, and admin URLs—knowing which to test avoids false negatives. You will also learn to reason about storage choices: when Ceph replaces Swift or backs Cinder, what changes in performance and failure domains should you expect. Finally, you will learn to design an overcloud with control plane redundancy and consider day-two operations using Ansible and Red Hat lifecycle tools. Each of these outcomes is tied to a competency milestone so you can confirm mastery by mapping services to a deployment plan and running endpoint inspections. screens.title: OpenStack as a Collection of Services
screens.subtitle: How modular services compose a cloud operating system

narration.text: OpenStack is not a single monolithic program; it is a set of specialized services that interoperate to present cloud capabilities. That modularity is central: each service owns a specific domain and exposes A P I endpoints that other services and users consume. Keystone is the identity authority; without valid tokens and service catalogs issued by Keystone, other services cannot authenticate requests. Nova manages the lifecycle of virtual machines: it schedules, boots, and terminates instances, coordinating with hypervisors. Glance stores and serves images that Nova uses to boot instances. Neutron provides the networking primitives—networks, subnets, routers, floating IPs and security groups—so tenant workloads can be isolated and connected. Storage is split into block (Cinder) and object (Swift). They provide different durability, access patterns and integration points. Horizon offers a web dashboard for interacting with these services, and while convenient, it is an A P I client and not the source of truth. Underneath, services persist state into a database and communicate via a message queue for asynchronous operations. A common mistake is treating Horizon as the control plane rather than an administrative UI; remember the APIs and services are the authoritative path. For architects, this model means failures are scoped to services and careful placement and redundancy of each service keep the cloud available. Consider a simple example where a Nova A P I node fails: if the message queue and database remain, control plane operations can be resumed from other Nova cells or replicas once the node is restored, illustrating the value of distributed services and clear ownership.

keyIdea.title: Service ownership
keyIdea.text: Each OpenStack service owns a domain and exposes APIs; the UI is a client, while Keystone, message queue, and DB are shared foundations.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › OpenStack as Services
Modular Service Model
Each service focuses on one domain and exposes APIs to other services and users.
Identity — Keystone
Authentication, tokens, service catalog and role management.
Compute — Nova
Instance lifecycle orchestration and scheduling to hypervisors.
Image — Glance
Repository for virtual disk images used to boot VMs.
Networking — Neutron
Virtual networks, routers, and security primitives for tenant isolation.
Key Takeaway

Design around service responsibilities: reduce blast radius by isolating service failures and automating recovery paths.

Supporting Foundations
Message queue and database coordinate state and asynchronous operations across services.
Message Queue
Used for asynchronous work coordination. Commonly RabbitMQ in RHOSP deployments.
Database
Services store authoritative state in MariaDB or PostgreSQL; consistent backups and replication are essential.
Common misconception
Thinking Horizon is the control plane. Horizon is a UI client; APIs and services are the control plane and remain authoritative.

screens.title: How Services Coordinate: Message Queue and Database
screens.subtitle: The control-plane coordination mechanisms

narration.text: OpenStack services need two coordination primitives: a message queue for asynchronous tasks and a database for durable state. The message queue handles background work such as instance build notifications, live-migration tasks, and inter-service signals. For example, when the scheduler decides where to place a VM, it posts notifications that compute nodes consume to begin provisioning. RabbitMQ is a common choice for that message bus in Red Hat OpenStack Platform. The database holds persistent state: user accounts, project metadata, instance records, and configuration data. Typical deployments use MariaDB or PostgreSQL with replication and backups. These two mechanisms play distinct roles: the queue moves ephemeral work items and orders operations, while the database is the canonical source of truth for long-lived records. A common error is under-provisioning the message queue; this can create backlogs that delay instance provisioning even when compute and storage are healthy. Another pitfall is inconsistent database replication setup, which can lead to split-brain or stale records. In practice, design your control plane with redundant message queue and database replicas, and monitor both queues and replication lag. This ensures that asynchronous work will continue and state remains consistent across control-plane nodes.

keyIdea.title: Queue vs Database
keyIdea.text: Message queues move work; databases store durable state. Both must be redundant and monitored to keep control-plane operations healthy.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Message Queue & DB
Coordination Primitives
How asynchronous work and durable state keep services synchronized.
Message Queue (e.g., RabbitMQ)
Moves tasks and notifications between services; handles asynchronous, ordered work that doesn't belong in the DB.
Database (MariaDB/PostgreSQL)
Stores authoritative records: users, projects, instance metadata, and configuration required for consistent operations.
Common mistake
Treating the queue as durable storage. Queues can drop or reorder messages if not configured correctly; rely on the database for canonical state.
Design tip: ensure separated, redundant control-plane nodes for both message queue and DB and monitor queue depths and replication lag during upgrades and peak operations.
Example: VM provisioning
Scheduler enqueues placement decisions, compute nodes consume tasks, and the database records instance state transitions. If the queue is backlogged, provisioning stalls despite healthy compute nodes.
Key Takeaway

Both primitives are essential and require redundancy; design them as first-class control-plane services.

narration.text: Keystone is the identity service and forms the security backbone for OpenStack. It issues authentication tokens, manages users, projects (tenants) and roles, and provides a service catalog that lists A P I endpoints for other services. For an architect, understanding Keystone means recognizing it as a gatekeeper: if Keystone is misconfigured, A P I calls across the cloud will fail authentication, even when individual services are healthy. A concrete example: when an operator requests a token and uses it to call the Nova A P I, Nova consults Keystone to validate the token and determine the caller's project and roles. If the service catalog lists incorrect URLs, clients will call the wrong endpoints or fail to reach a service. A common misconception is assuming tokens are long-lived credentials; by default they are short-lived to reduce risk and should be renewed or obtained programmatically. For availability, Keystone must be deployed redundantly with a replicated database to avoid single points of failure. In practice, plan Keystone replication and ensure the service catalog entries are accurate during deploy and upgrades. A short verification step is to request a token and then list services; if that succeeds, both authentication and catalog are functioning as expected. This confirms your control plane basics are operating.

keyIdea.title: Keystone is critical
keyIdea.text: Keystone controls authentication and the service catalog; its availability and correct configuration are prerequisites for a functioning cloud.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Keystone
Keystone Responsibilities
Authentication, identity, service catalog, and role mapping.
Tokens and sessions
Keystone issues short-lived tokens used by APIs to authorize requests and determine scoped access.
Service catalog
A central index of service endpoints. Accurate catalog entries ensure clients and services reach the intended API URLs.
Misconception
Treating Keystone as optional. Without Keystone, service authentication and catalog lookups fail and APIs become inaccessible.
Key Takeaway

Design Keystone with redundancy and reliable DB replication; verify token issuance and catalog entries during deployment validation.

Concrete Test
Request a token using the OpenStack client, then list services. If both succeed, Keystone authentication and catalog discovery are functional.
# source overcloudrc
# openstack token issue
# openstack service list

screens.title: Nova — Compute Lifecycle
screens.subtitle: Scheduling, provisioning, and instance lifecycle management

narration.text: Nova is the compute service responsible for managing the entire lifecycle of virtual machine instances. It receives A P I requests to create, resize, migrate, or delete instances and coordinates with the scheduler, conductor, and hypervisor drivers to perform those actions. Nova is central to cloud operations because it maps user requests to available compute resources. For example, when a user requests a new VM, Nova's scheduler evaluates available hosts, taking into account flavors, resource limits, and policies. After placement, compute services on hypervisors perform the actual provisioning. A misconception is thinking Nova directly stores long-term instance metadata; while it records state in the database, operational state also flows through the message queue during asynchronous tasks. For high availability, you should distribute Nova A P I and scheduler services across multiple controller nodes and consider nova cell configurations to isolate compute groups. Understand that Nova integrates with Glance to fetch images, with Neutron to attach networking, and with Cinder for volume attachments. This interconnected behavior means changes to networking or image availability impact instance lifecycle; testing end-to-end provisioning validates that Nova interacts correctly with image, network, and storage services.

keyIdea.title: Nova coordinates compute
keyIdea.text: Nova orchestrates scheduling and lifecycle actions and depends on Glance, Neutron, Cinder and the control-plane primitives for reliable provisioning.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Nova
Compute Lifecycle
Scheduling, provisioning, and coordinating resources for instances.
Scheduler & placement
Evaluates resource availability and policies to choose hosts for instances.
Workers and hypervisors
Compute services on hypervisors execute the actual VM operations as directed by Nova control plane messages.
Integration note
Nova works with Glance for images, Neutron for networking, and Cinder for block attachments; orchestration requires all three to be reachable and correct.
Key Takeaway

Ensure Nova services are distributed and that supporting services—image, network, storage—are reliable to avoid failed instance operations.

Concrete scenario
A VM fails to boot because Glance is unreachable. Nova requests the image, receives an error, and the instance transitions to an error state. Fixing image availability restores provisioning flow.
# Example validation
openstack server create --image IMAGE --flavor FLAVOR --nic net-id=NET --security-group default INSTANCE

narration.text: Glance is the image service that stores virtual disk images and makes them available to Nova and other services. Images are the templates used to create new virtual machines, so Glance must ensure availability and integrity of these artifacts. For example, when an administrator uploads a golden image for a Linux distribution, Glance stores metadata and the binary image so instances can boot from it. Glance does not manage running instances; it supplies static templates while Nova handles lifecycle. An important practical note: ensure image visibility and access rights are set appropriately for projects and that the image backend has sufficient performance for your expected boot storms. In Red Hat deployments you will often place images on a backend with fast access or use caching strategies to avoid repeated cold pulls. A common misconception is expecting Glance to provide block-level snapshot storage; Glance manages disk images as objects or files and integrates with Cinder for block volume snapshots. Test image uploads and retrievals during deployment to validate the image service and backend performance. Confirming image fetch times and visibility in the service catalog avoids slower boot times and availability surprises during scale events.

keyIdea.title: Glance provides templates
keyIdea.text: Glance stores and serves VM images; ensure correct visibility, backend performance, and integration with Nova for predictable instance boots.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Glance
Image Repository
Store, catalog, and serve virtual disk images used to boot instances.
Image lifecycle
Upload, set metadata and visibility, version images, and retire old templates as needed.
Performance considerations
Backends and caching affect image fetch times during instance boot storms; plan placement accordingly.
Key Takeaway

Treat Glance as a catalog of templates and validate image visibility and fetch performance as part of deployment tests.

Concrete Example
Upload an image, mark it public for a test project, then boot multiple instances to measure startup times and backend load. Use this to tune cache or backend placement.
# glance image-create --name "centos-golden" --file centos.qcow2 --disk-format qcow2 --container-format bare
# openstack image list

screens.title: Neutron — Networking as a Service
screens.subtitle: Virtual networks, routers, and tenant isolation

narration.text: Neutron provides network connectivity for OpenStack workloads. It exposes APIs for creating networks, subnets, routers, floating IPs and security groups, enabling flexible and isolated tenant networking. As an architect, you must decide which networking plugins and backends to use and how networking is mapped to physical infrastructure. Neutron abstracts virtual networks from physical switches, but that abstraction requires careful mapping of VLANs, overlays, or provider networks to avoid MTU issues and ensure performance. A common operational challenge is ensuring security group rules and tenant router configurations match expected traffic flows; mismatches can block services even if compute and storage are healthy. Integration points are important: Nova uses Neutron to attach ports and assign IPs, and networking state is referenced during instance provisioning. For high availability, place Neutron server components redundantly and verify that the agent layer on compute nodes is consistent and compatible with your chosen backend. A practical example is creating a tenant network with a DHCP-enabled subnet and then launching an instance that receives an IP. If DHCP fails, instances will boot without network connectivity; diagnosing the Neutron agents and DHCP namespace quickly isolates the fault. Plan network design alongside storage and compute to ensure predictable tenant connectivity and performance.

keyIdea.title: Network design matters
keyIdea.text: Neutron abstracts tenant networks but requires careful backend mapping and agent consistency to ensure isolation, performance and availability.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Neutron
Networking as a Service
APIs and agents that create virtual networks, subnets, routers and security controls for tenants.
Virtual networks & backends
Choose between overlay networks, VLANs, or provider networks and ensure mapping to physical switches is consistent.
Agent layer
Neutron agents on compute and network nodes implement forwarding, DHCP, and NAT; agent mismatches cause outages.
Misconception
Assuming virtual networks are automatically optimized for performance. MTU, overlay encapsulation and physical mapping affect throughput and must be tested.
Key Takeaway

Plan networking backends and agent configuration during design; test DHCP, floating IPs, and security group behavior in a staging environment.

Concrete scenario
Create a tenant network and subnet, boot an instance and verify it receives an IP and can reach a test endpoint. If not, inspect DHCP and agent logs to find where the network request was dropped.
# openstack network create tenant-net
# openstack subnet create --network tenant-net --subnet-range 192.0.2.0/24 tenant-subnet
# openstack server create --image IMAGE --flavor FLAVOR --nic net-id=$(openstack network show tenant-net -f value -c id) INST

screens.title: Cinder, Swift and Ceph — Storage Roles and Integrations
screens.subtitle: Block, object, and unified storage strategies

narration.text: OpenStack separates storage into block and object domains. Cinder provides persistent block storage volumes that attach to instances, while Swift offers an eventually consistent object store for unstructured data like backups and archives. Red Hat OpenStack Platform commonly integrates Ceph as a unified backend that can satisfy both block and object needs and can offer improved performance and data protection techniques like replication and erasure coding. When architecting storage, understand trade-offs: block volumes are suitable for VM disks requiring POSIX-like block access, while object storage is ideal for immutable artifacts and large-scale archive data. Integrating Ceph changes operational patterns: administrators manage Ceph pools and integration points so that Cinder and the Swift A P I can use the same storage cluster. A common misconception is that using Ceph removes the need for storage planning; Ceph introduces its own capacity and OSD considerations and must be tuned for expected input and output patterns. For HA and scale, distribute storage services and plan for recovery and rebalancing operations. A practical example: using Ceph RBD-backed volumes for Cinder yields flexible snapshotting and cloning, improving VM provisioning times for certain workloads. Test backup and restore procedures for both block and object data to ensure your planned storage strategy meets recovery objectives.

keyIdea.title: Choose storage by need
keyIdea.text: Cinder for block, Swift for object, and Ceph as a unified backend—each choice affects performance, operations, and recovery strategies.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Storage Comparison
Block vs Object vs Unified
Understand when to use Cinder, Swift or Ceph for your workloads.
Cinder (Block)
Persistent volumes for VM disks that can be attached and snapshotted independently of instance lifecycle.
Swift (Object)
Distributed object store for backups, archives, and large unstructured datasets.
Ceph Integration
Ceph can present RBD for Cinder and an object interface compatible with Swift, unifying storage management and enabling replication and erasure coding for resilience.
Key Takeaway

Match storage function to workload: volumes for block I/O, objects for large unstructured data, and consider Ceph when you need a unified, scalable backend.

Concrete Example
Use Ceph-backed Cinder volumes for a database VM that needs snapshotting and cloning. Use Swift or Ceph object interface for nightly backups and static media storage.
Operational note: verify Ceph pool configuration and OSD capacity planning before migrating production workloads to a Ceph-backed storage model.

screens.title: Horizon — The Dashboard
screens.subtitle: A web UI for managing OpenStack resources

narration.text: Horizon is the web-based dashboard for OpenStack and gives administrators and users a GUI to interact with services. While Horizon is convenient for quick inspections and simple operations, it is a client that calls the same APIs you would use from the command line or automation. As an architect, you should treat Horizon as a useful tool for exploration and demonstration, but not as the authoritative automation path for repeatable operations or complex workflows. For example, day-two automation and consistent change management are better achieved with Ansible playbooks that call OpenStack APIs or with TripleO workflows for lifecycle tasks. A common mistake is relying on Horizon for large-scale or scripted changes; UI actions are harder to reproduce reliably across environments. Ensure Horizon is installed, reachable, and points to the correct service catalog entries during validation. Confirm it reflects real project and resource states by cross-checking with A P I queries. Horizon also surfaces some operator-level settings, but any critical production task should be codified and tested through automation to ensure predictable, auditable operations. Think of Horizon as a helpful inspection pane rather than a deployment tool.

keyIdea.title: Horizon is a client
keyIdea.text: Use Horizon for inspection and small admin tasks, but rely on automation and APIs for repeatability and production operations.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Horizon
Horizon Dashboard
A UI client for interacting with OpenStack APIs and resources.
Use cases
Quick inspection of projects, launching single instances, and visual confirmation of resources.
Limitations
Not designed for large-scale automation or repeatable day-two operations; prefer Ansible and API-based workflows for those tasks.
Key Takeaway

Treat Horizon as an administrative client for inspection and demonstration; codify production tasks in automation for repeatability.

Practical check
Open Horizon, confirm you can list instances and networks, then repeat the same checks using the OpenStack client to verify parity and catalog accuracy.

narration.text: TripleO, short for OpenStack on OpenStack, is Red Hat's recommended approach to deploy and manage an OpenStack control plane. The pattern uses an undercloud—an OpenStack installation that acts as a deployment engine—to provision and manage the overcloud, which is your production OpenStack environment. The undercloud runs orchestration and provisioning services that call image, compute, network and bare-metal provisioning APIs to build the overcloud nodes. This approach offers consistent, repeatable deployments and simplifies upgrades because the same cloud management principles are used to manage the platform itself. For example, the undercloud can image and provision controller and compute nodes, configure services, and register endpoints in Keystone. A common mistake is treating TripleO as a simple installer; instead it is a management plane that you must operate and plan for. You should provision the undercloud with redundancy and ensure it has access to necessary backends like Ceph during overcloud configuration. TripleO also integrates with Ansible for day-two operations, enabling automation of routine tasks. Practically, when designing your deployment, map the roles of undercloud components and plan network connectivity and storage access to ensure the overcloud can be built reliably and maintained consistently over time.

keyIdea.title: Undercloud manages overcloud
keyIdea.text: TripleO uses an undercloud to provision and manage the production overcloud, enabling consistent automation and lifecycle operations for RHOSP.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › TripleO
TripleO Deployment Model
Use an undercloud to deploy and manage the production overcloud, enabling automation and repeatable lifecycle operations.
Undercloud purpose
A management OpenStack instance used to image, provision and configure the production environment.
Overcloud outcome
The production cloud—controller, compute and storage nodes—managed by the undercloud for ongoing operations.
Misconception
TripleO is not a one-time installer. It remains as a management plane you operate for upgrades and lifecycle tasks.
Key Takeaway

Treat the undercloud as an operational component; secure and scale it appropriately since it manages lifecycle tasks for the production cloud.

Practical note
Ensure the undercloud has network access to provision PXE, and to any storage backends like Ceph that are required during overcloud configuration.

screens.title: Designing for High Availability and Scalability
screens.subtitle: Patterns to remove single points of failure and scale operations

narration.text: Designing a highly available and scalable OpenStack environment requires thinking in layers: control plane, data plane, and supporting infrastructure. For the control plane, replicate A P I services and run redundant message queue and database clusters. Distribute Keystone, Glance, Nova A P I nodes, and Neutron servers across controller nodes so that any single node failure does not take down the cloud. For the data plane, scale compute by adding hypervisors in a cell or compute pool rather than overloading a few hosts. Storage should be architected for redundancy: Ceph offers replication and erasure coding that protect data and enable OSD failures to be tolerated without service loss. Network design must plan for agent redundancy and consistent mapping of overlay to physical networks. Operationally, automate provisioning and day-two tasks using TripleO and Ansible so upgrades and configuration changes are repeatable. Monitor key metrics: queue depth, DB replication lag, OSD health, and agent status. A common design mistake is underestimating recovery time during rebalancing after a storage failure; plan capacity buffers and test failover scenarios. A concrete exercise is to plan a controller node count and database replica layout, then simulate controller failure and observe how services failover and recover. The goal is to ensure continuous operation while keeping maintenance predictable and safe.

keyIdea.title: Layers of resilience
keyIdea.text: Redundancy across control plane services, scalable compute pools, and Ceph-backed storage form the basis of HA OpenStack designs.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › HA & Scalability
Patterns for Resilience
Distribute control-plane roles, scale compute via pools, and design storage for failure tolerance.
Control plane replication
Run multiple API and scheduler nodes and cluster your message queue and database for failover and capacity.
Compute scaling
Add hypervisors into cells or pools instead of overloading a small set of hosts to increase capacity safely.
Storage durability
Use replication or erasure coding with Ceph and plan capacity for rebalancing during OSD failures.
Key Takeaway

Plan redundancy, test failover, and automate operations to keep the cloud available and maintainable at scale.

narration.text: This hands-on activity shows how to verify service availability and endpoints using the OpenStack client. First, source the environment file such as overcloudrc to load credentials. This makes the client authenticate against Keystone and receive a token. Next, run the command to list registered services; this returns names and types like nova (compute) and glance (image) so you can confirm which services are registered. Then list endpoints to view public, internal and admin URLs for each service. Filtering endpoints by service, for example by 'compute', helps you inspect Nova's A P I URLs specifically. This practice matters because endpoint discovery confirms that Keystone's service catalog matches your intended deployment topology and that clients will reach correct addresses. A common mistake is assuming endpoints pointing to localhost or internal test names are correct for external access; verify the public URL is reachable from user-facing networks. In the provided code template, the commands are shown as typical examples to run in a deployment environment; in lab work, compare the returned URL entries to your inventory and resolve any mismatches. Finally, use endpoint checks as a fast initial troubleshooting step when an A P I appears down: if the endpoint is missing or incorrect, focus on Keystone and registration rather than every downstream service.

keyIdea.title: Endpoint verification
keyIdea.text: Listing services and endpoints with the OpenStack client is a quick, practical check that validates Keystone catalog and service accessibility.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Service Endpoints
Activity: Inspect Endpoints
Use the OpenStack client to list services and endpoints and validate deployment registrations.
# source ~/overcloudrc

# openstack endpoint list
# openstack endpoint list --service compute
Expected output shows service ID, name, type and a table of endpoints with region and URL. Compare public/internal/admin URLs against your inventory.
Key Takeaway

Endpoint inspection is your fastest initial check for API accessibility and Keystone catalog correctness during validation and troubleshooting.

Troubleshooting tip
If endpoints are missing or incorrect, verify service registration jobs in TripleO or your deployment tooling and confirm Keystone has the right catalog entries before checking downstream service logs.

narration.text: These compact concept cards distill the chapter to three essential ideas you should keep front-of-mind. First, Keystone is the identity authority; it issues tokens and the service catalog and must be redundant because it gatekeeps all A P I access. Second, Nova is the compute orchestrator; it schedules and manages VM lifecycle and depends on Glance, Neutron and Cinder to complete provisioning. Third, storage choices matter: Cinder and Swift provide block and object semantics, while Ceph can unify backends and bring replication and erasure coding. Hold these concepts as you design deployments: ensure Keystone availability, distribute Nova and A P I services, and pick a storage model that matches workload and recovery goals. A quick check you can do in any deployment is to request a token and list service endpoints; if those succeed, your basic control-plane registration is correct. Carry these core ideas forward when planning HA, integrations and automation.

narration.text: These three operational reminders capture Red Hat's approach to deploying and operating OpenStack. First, TripleO uses an undercloud to deploy and manage the overcloud—treat the undercloud as an operational component that requires its own availability and connectivity. Second, automation and lifecycle tools like Ansible and Red Hat lifecycle products are essential for day-two operations; avoid manual changes for repeatable tasks. Third, validate integrations such as Ceph and ensure you plan capacity and rebalancing for storage backends. A simple operational check is to source your overcloud credentials and list services and endpoints; this verifies that Keystone, service registration and basic A P I accessibility are functioning.
